verses.note: The great lights rule, but only because God set them in place and assigned them their work. Throughout Scripture authority in creation is derived authority, given by God and answerable to him.

God reserves vengeance to himself (Deuteronomy 32:35) and restrains the spiral of blood feud. The guilty man is judged, yet his life is protected, a mercy the chapter's next murderer, Lamech, will twist into a boast.
The flood is not a natural disaster God failed to prevent but a judgment he brings. Psalm 29:10 turns this into worship: the God who sat enthroned over the flood still reigns as king forever.

God's descent shows the true scale of the project. However high human work reaches, God stands above it and sees it for what it is. Psalm 2 draws the same picture of the nations plotting while the One enthroned in heaven looks on.
The builders' strength lay in their common speech, and God reaches it with a word. The verse shows that human capacities, language included, are held within God's rule and can be limited by him.
The one who blesses Abram is the owner of heaven and earth, not the patron of one city. The victory over four kings is set inside the rule of the God to whom every land and king already belongs.

Melchizedek says God "has delivered your enemies into your hand". The battle of verse 15 was Abram's fight, but the verse credits the outcome to God, a pattern that runs through Israel's holy war accounts.

God announces the outcome before either child is born, and it overturns the custom that the firstborn leads. Paul uses exactly this timing in Romans 9:11-12: the word came before the twins had done anything good or bad, so that God's purpose would stand by his calling.

Rebekah acts because she understands that the blessing given before the LORD will be binding. The story will show that God's purpose, announced before the twins' birth, is achieved, but it never suggests that God needed her scheme to achieve it.

Many interpreters read Isaac's great trembling as the moment he realizes that God has overruled his plan. His refusal to revoke the blessing shows him submitting, at last, to the word spoken before the twins were born. Hebrews 11:20 treats the blessing as an act of faith.
